source: AA-S2#early-to-middle (chorus-chords passage; 'had the lyric before I knew' passage; second-verse passage)
finding: Carpenter says she already had the repeated title phrase before she knew what the song would be about. The phrase came out of a situation she was living through that week. The session's starting point was Antonoff's chorus chords: he played, watched what made her light up (and noticed when she pulled a face), and the phrase was matched to those chords. Carpenter also says she and Amy Allen wrote the second verse in about five minutes while Antonoff was changing the key, with Antonoff moving between instruments as the two of them worked on the words.
why_it_matters: A title phrase that a writer is already carrying around can wait for the right chord bed. The person playing can steer by watching the singer react, without arguing for an idea.
when_not: This is one session in which the artist brought her own phrase; it says nothing about rooms where no one arrives with a phrase.

source: AA-S2#~0.02, ~0.20, ~0.76, ~0.87 and the bridge passage (~two-thirds through)
finding: Carpenter says the subject (swinging between confidence and embarrassment over a man) was picked because she could frame it as funny. She describes needing to laugh while talking about something you could cry about, and calls the result 'desperately comical'. Antonoff says the best artists know when to be funny because it makes the next sad line sadder. In the bridge, which was missing at the end of the first day and finished about a month later at his LA studio, a sincere, heartbreaking line is followed straight away by a line that undercuts it with a joke. Antonoff calls that pairing the genius of her writing.
quote: all my favorite artists know exactly when to be funny
why_it_matters: Put the sincere line first and the joke right after it, so the laugh follows the hurt and makes it stronger instead of covering it.
when_not: My own inference, not from a source: if every line is a joke there is no sincere line for the humour to sharpen.

source: AA-S2#~0.50-0.60 (conversation and acting passages; melody-ending passage)
finding: Antonoff says many of the lyrics on these songs are literal things Carpenter said in conversation, and Carpenter agrees the song is really a conversation with herself. She says she treats singing as acting and pictures talking to the person as she sings, which lets her move between sung and spoken phrasing. She says she likes a line that is sung sweetly and then turns blunt two seconds later, and credits the give-it-to-them-straight women she grew up with, including her mother. She also says one melody ending was moved from high to low so the delivery would land. That is a text-only report; I have not heard the audio.
why_it_matters: Write down what the artist actually says in the room word for word, because the lyric may already be in it, and sing it as if speaking to someone rather than as a statement.
when_not: Speech copied straight into a lyric still has to fit the melody's stresses; Carpenter's note about moving a melody ending lower shows the delivery being adjusted to suit the words.

finding: Allen says that in sessions a flag often goes up that a line or note is too weird, too pop, too personal, or too specific and niche. She says that flagged part is usually the best part of the song, that people love it nine times out of ten, and that she tries to chase those moments. Her example is a profane word in Please Please Please that the writers laughed at, which became one of the most-loved parts of the song.
quote: usually the best part of the song
why_it_matters: The line the room is nervous about is a candidate to keep and test, not one to cut automatically.
when_not: Critics quoted on Wikipedia about Man's Best Friend (AA-S21: Slant, the Guardian, the Independent) said the profanity and innuendo were overused, so chasing the nervous line can tip into sameness.

finding: Allen says that when writing with artists she always starts with the chorus, which she calls the crux of the song. If someone later wants to redo the chorus, her instinct is that they should probably write a new song. For her own 2024 album she deliberately dropped chorus-first and wrote straight through from the first word to the last, as she did when she was younger, to break pop-song rules she had absorbed.
why_it_matters: In a co-write, settle the chorus first because everything else hangs off it. Writing from the top down is a deliberate alternative when the aim is a personal song rather than a hit.
when_not: Her own album shows she drops chorus-first when she is writing for herself.

finding: Allen says it was not really a disagreement, but a couple of weeks after the session McRae said she thought the chorus lyric was wrong. They then edited the song heavily and, in Allen's words, completely changed its concept. Allen says she trusts the artist because the artist has to sing the song for years and knows her own voice best. The only documented before-and-after facts are that the chorus lyric and the concept changed. Wikipedia (AA-S24) separately reports McRae saying a chorus line was reworded and that the song was rewritten and recorded in January 2023; no wording is available to me.
why_it_matters: When the artist rejects the chorus after the session, expect the concept to change rather than a word or two, and give the artist's ear for her own voice the final say.
when_not: This applies when writing for an artist; for a writer's own record there is no artist to defer to.

finding: Allen says she is notoriously bad at writing from a title someone hands her or from a planned idea; a title out of thin air feels like a puzzle to solve. She prefers to talk with the artist about what is going on in their life and stumble on the song from there. She also says she has spent the last couple of years trying to undo structural habits, for example when someone says a song should go straight to the chorus, because a song does not need every trick every time.
quote: it feels like I'm trying to do a Sudoku puzzle
why_it_matters: For this writer the title comes out of talking with the artist, not from a list of titles, and a missing section is sometimes the better choice.
when_not: Other writers do work from title lists; this is her stated preference, not a general rule.

source: AA-S5#Q&A answer to 'Some of the lyrics on Man's Best Friend are hilarious'
finding: Allen describes the Man's Best Friend sessions with Carpenter as swinging from vulnerable conversation to hysterical laughter within a minute. She says the two of them would look at each other and ask whether they were really going to say a line, then decide that they were. On Manchild, she credits Carpenter's self-awareness for a song that is melodic and beautiful but full of witty remarks that poke fun at herself. She does not describe how Manchild was written.
quote: Oh my God, are we going to say that?!
why_it_matters: Treat the moment both writers hesitate over a line as a decision to make out loud, and keep the line if both agree.
when_not: See AA-F4 for the critics' counterpoint about overuse.

finding: Allen says she did not know humour was something she could express in her writing until she met Carpenter. She says Carpenter was the first artist to invite her into her highs and lows while staying witty, and she places this in a line running back to Dolly Parton and John Prine. She says Adore You taught her that a song does not have to be serious and heart-wrenching. She also says she was taught that too many chords or too-personal lyrics lose listeners, and she cites the key changes on Carpenter's last two albums as proof that this is wrong.
quote: the listener is way more than capable of following you
why_it_matters: Humour and harmonic surprise are allowed in a hit, and listeners will follow an unexpected turn.

source: AA-S8#Q 'How did you and your co-writers write this song?' and Q 'How did this song come together?'
finding: Allen says Back to You started the night before the session, when she reconnected with a friend and thought about that relationship. The next morning she sang the co-writers (Micah Premnath and Trackside) a melody and an idea, and they wrote the song quickly. On Halsey's Without Me she says the writers were not trying to write an empowerment song; it became one. She notes that songs written as empowerment songs can come out cheesy or preachy.
quote: I sang them a melody and an idea I had.
why_it_matters: A melody plus the seed of an idea, both carried in from the writer's own life, can be enough to start a fast session. A theme like empowerment comes out better as a result than as the goal.
when_not: This is one documented melody-first case; no source I fetched has Allen calling herself generally melody-first or lyric-first.

source: AA-S9#Q&A 'Most of your songs are pretty dark' and 'Why do indie rock artists make such good pop songwriters'
finding: Allen says she usually reaches for harder emotions first and writes from something she is dealing with at the time. With artists, she listens for a subject they keep coming back to and writes from that. She writes with a guitar in hand, aiming for songs that could stand up on stage, and says you could strip the production off her co-writes and hear an indie rock song.
quote: I instantly go to something I'm dealing with right now
why_it_matters: Listen for the subject the artist keeps returning to in conversation and test whether the song works on one guitar before production.
when_not: She calls Adore You her first feel-good song, so the dark-first habit has exceptions.

finding: In this AP story, the account of how Espresso was written comes from co-writer and producer Julian Bunetta, not from Allen. He says the four writers (Carpenter, Allen, Steph Jones, Bunetta) were like kids having fun, laughing and playing, and links that energy to the song's cheerful sound and its nonsensical lines. Separately, Carpenter (AA-S16, NME relaying Apple Music and Vogue) says comparing an infatuation to a caffeine habit was fun to write and that the song captures a moment of unusual confidence. Allen gives no account of writing it in any source I could open.
quote: were kids having fun and laughing and playing
why_it_matters: A playful room can produce a hook that does not quite make sense on paper; the playfulness of the session is what produces it.
when_not: Nonsense needs confident delivery and a clear central image (here caffeine as infatuation); otherwise it reads as filler.

finding: Press coverage relayed on Wikipedia treats the chorus phrase as grammatically odd. Them discussed with a grammar writer whether it parses as one noun phrase or two side by side, and a linguist consulted by Vulture suggested it is not grammatical. Yet Vulture called the hook an instant earworm and the lyrics whimsical, and the phrase became a meme. The feature is a coffee noun used where an adjective or noun phrase would normally go, so the phrase holds attention because it does not quite parse. I could not open the original Vulture and Them pieces, so this is second-hand.
why_it_matters: A hook can work because it is slightly broken grammar delivered with total confidence, which makes listeners repeat it and argue about it.
when_not: My own inference: it works where the persona is confident and playful; in a sincere ballad the same oddness would read as a mistake.

finding: Press relayed on Wikipedia describes the song's language as insults delivered over sweet, upbeat melodies (People), as 'withering couplets' (Pitchfork), and as Carpenter comically laying into an ex (Variety). The page also notes a sarcastic tone in the intro. Billboard reports Carpenter's own description of the man in four blunt insulting adjectives. Allen (AA-F8) adds that the song also makes fun of the narrator herself. Together these describe a sweet melody carrying contempt, softened by the narrator mocking herself too.
why_it_matters: Sarcasm goes down more easily when the tune is sweet and the narrator turns some of the mockery on herself.
when_not: Wikipedia gives no source for the 'sarcastic intro' description, and I did not open the Pitchfork, People or Variety reviews directly.

finding: No source I fetched describes Please Please Please as a plea that turns into a threat. Wikipedia's summary of the NYT, LA Times and Guardian reading is a famous woman's anxiety that her partner will embarrass her. My inference: the repeated polite title (a plea) combined with Carpenter's stated liking for being sung sweetly and then blunt two seconds later (AA-S2) is what lets the request carry a warning. The politeness is in the title, and the edge comes from what she asks him not to do. This reading is mine and not attributed to any writer.
why_it_matters: A polite repeated request can carry a warning if the verses spell out the consequence instead of the chorus.
when_not: Do not present this as the writers' intent; nobody in the fetched sources says it.
